_comment: Aelgard Heartlands bestiary. Curated deep-bible entries mirroring data/npc-bibles.json. Each monster carries voice/ecology/lore so the region feels lived-in. The stat spine lives in src/content/aelgard/monsters-mega.js + monsters-blitz*.js; this file is the design bible the codex/narrator/slayer-master read from. Anti-generic: no WoW-flavoured mobs.
_region_tone: ploughed, tax-tired, yeast-and-rain. Threats are social-economic: debt enforcers, inheritance feuds, roads gone unsafe because the militia is thin.

monsters.name: Farmhand brigand
monsters.examine: A sour farmhand turned bandit. Has opinions about taxes.
bible: Sons of sharecroppers who missed the Crown's winter levy. They are not killers by trade; they are killers by arithmetic. Most carry their late father's belt-knife and a pitchfork with the tines filed to points.

They haunt the stone-walls west of the Heartlands toll bridge, and will let a known Heartlander pass in daylight — it is strangers and night that turn them. They speak a flat shire dialect, drop t's, and say 'owings' where others say 'debts.'

If cornered, a brigand will often throw down and ask for water before he asks for mercy. If allowed to live, he will return to banditry within a fortnight. Alden knows all their names and writes none of them down.
monsters.habitat: hedge-lined lanes, toll road, abandoned threshing sheds
monsters.anti_pattern_note: do not reskin as a 'generic bandit.' The wrinkle is that each brigand has a farm of origin and a debt letter pinned inside his jerkin.

monsters.name: Corn rat
monsters.examine: Fat on stolen grain. Too smug.
bible: A Heartlands corn rat is not the scurrying thing of town cellars; it is the granary king. Fed on a decade of good harvests, it grows to the size of a small badger and carries itself like a bailiff.

They bully mice, they bully cats, and they have been known to stare down farmhands at the silo door. Their fur is the exact oat-gold of the field they steal from, and their claws are dulled from gripping sacks.
The Hedgelords put a bounty of two copper per tail. The corn rats, in response, learned to leave their tails behind when fleeing — a trick farmers still argue about in the pubs.
monsters.habitat: grain silos, harvest sheds, field hedgerows
monsters.anti_pattern_note: starter slayer task at level 1. The bible teaches ecology, not combat.

monsters.name: Hedge boar
bible: A hedge boar is a wild hog that has lived so long in the thorn-walls between fields that the hedge has become part of it. Bramble-thorns twist into the pelt and fuse with the hide. Cutting one open, you find bramble-roots where ribs should be.

They are territorial about a specific hedge, not a range, and will charge any tall shape crossing it. Most Heartlands farmers know the hedges which 'have a boar in them' and will detour a full field to avoid one.
Hunter-tradition says you stab, never slash — a slash rings off the thorn-plate. The hide, stripped and cured, makes a pelt that shrugs arrows.
monsters.habitat: thorn hedgerows between long-standing field boundaries
monsters.reagent_callout: Hedgerow pelt feeds into Ranger Cloak upgrade at the Veilwood fletcher (see drop table).

monsters.name: Hedgerow stalker
monsters.examine: Crawls inside the hedges. Leaves little corridors of nothing.
bible: Not a species but a stage: a beast that has eaten enough hedge boars to be mostly hedge. The first sign is that birds no longer nest in a stretch of hedge; the second is that dogs will not walk past it.

Stalkers ambush by pulling a victim into the hedge-tunnel and suffocating them in thorn. The militia has a standing order to burn any hedge that has gone quiet for a week, but farmers resist, because a burned hedge takes a decade to re-grow and marks the boundary for lawsuits.
A stalker's heart is a hedgelord pin — a brass brooch passed down among the Hedgelord bandit fraternity, which each initiate swallows for reasons nobody sober remembers.
monsters.habitat: long stretches of silent hedge, bird-absent lanes
monsters.anti_pattern_note: this is a mid-tier predator; do not inflate its max_hit to turn it into a mini-boss. The scare is the ambush, not the stats.

monsters.name: Militia captain
monsters.examine: A veteran of the toll wars. Very tired.
bible: A captain only fights if you draw steel inside a Heartlands toll-house, or if the Crown ledger has your name. Otherwise he will walk past you and recommend the tea at the second pub along.

Captains wear the old pattern half-plate — the one that stopped being issued after the Sootworks campaign because it bent in at the shoulder under any hammer blow. Every captain knows this. Every captain wears it anyway.
Insignia are worth money in Moryskah and no money at all in the Heartlands. Alden refuses to count them as trophies.
monsters.habitat: toll-roads, tax houses, the south gate at dusk
monsters.reagent_callout: Militia insignia + Bronze kiteshield at Smith Kael = Heartlands watch-shield (modest ranged defence bonus).

monsters.name: Plough ghoul
monsters.examine: A field-hand who kept plowing after he died.
bible: A Heartlands mystery: men who die in a field at the harvest moon sometimes stand up the following dawn and finish the furrow. They remember the work, not their names. They do not speak. They do not eat.

The ghoul ploughs in straight lines across any terrain, including through walls and livestock. A farmer will, on discovering his grandfather ploughing an old field, leave him to it — it is considered unlucky to stop one.
Father Dorin blesses the fields every Sowing Friday to reduce the count. His success rate is real but small.
monsters.habitat: long-fallow fields, recently-ploughed winter soil, grave-adjacent farmland
monsters.anti_pattern_note: NOT a generic undead. Killing one on the field without permission is a social crime.

monsters.name: Toll-road highwayman
bible: Highwaymen run the stretch of toll-road between the Heartlands and the Moryskah border, where the Crown's writ gets thin and the weather gets damp. They work in pairs; one with a shortbow, one with a parley-smile.
They will take coin, rings, and good boots; they will not take a wedding band (bad luck), a farmer's seed satchel (bad trade), or any letter bearing a Sootworks crest (too dangerous to fence).
The senior of the pair usually has a toll-ticket folded in his jerkin — a real one — in case a patrol catches him up-road. Half the patrol waves him through.
monsters.habitat: the long toll-road, the Moryskah-side bridge, roadside inns after dark
monsters.drops_note: Tinker lockpick drop is intentionally rare — do not pool it with the brigand table.

monsters.name: Rat king
monsters.examine: A knot of rats bound by tail, hunger, and a crude crown.
bible: Seven to thirteen corn rats, tails knotted into a single writhing mass, moving as one. A rat king forms only in the deepest grain-silos after three failed harvests. It is a sign, old farmers say, of a year that wants watching.

The 'crown' is real — the rats begin with it by accident (a bit of pewter mouse-trap, usually) and keep it through instinct; the king is the rat with the crown, though which rat that is changes hourly.
Killing a rat king counts as a municipal service. The mayor pays in coin; Father Dorin pays in blessing. Both claim the other should pay more.
monsters.habitat: abandoned silos, cellar warrens, the collapsed floor of the Heartlands granary
monsters.reagent_callout: Rat king drops the first Heartlands encounter-unique: the Hedgelord pin at 1/512, which combines with an old brass-buckled belt to make the Hedgelord's belt (prayer-point bonus).

monsters.name: Sow-witch
monsters.examine: Keeps pigs that answer to names, not whistles.
bible: A sow-witch is, by Heartlands common law, still a citizen. She pays the toll, she pays the tithe, and she does not poach. What she does do is keep four pigs who come when called by name — which is widely considered a moral crime, even if no statute covers it.

The witches live in single-room cottages on the edge of woods, drink nettle tea, and trade blessings for bacon. They will curse a thief but not a tax-collector. Their magic is rooted in names: they can curse a thing only if they know what you call it.
Sow-witches keep grimy guam and marrentill in jars. The jars are for sale at fair prices. Shoplifters get named pigs set on them.
monsters.habitat: woodland edges, one-room cottages with four muddy pigs
monsters.anti_pattern_note: the pigs DO come help her — do not ignore the swarm mechanic on spawn.

monsters.name: Church gargoyle
monsters.examine: Carved for a belltower. Moved when the bell stopped.
bible: The Heartlands Chapel lost its bell in the Sootworks campaign — melted for shot. After, three of the six carved gargoyles on the belltower climbed down and took up residence in the churchyard. They have not moved in twenty-two years. Moss grows on them. Birds nest in their mouths.
They are not hostile. They will not attack the devout, the elderly, or a dog. They will defend the churchyard from desecration with a brutality that has ended two grave-robber lives in living memory.
Father Dorin considers them parishioners and counts them in the midsummer census. He does not give them seats in the pew, however, because the floorboards will not bear it.
monsters.anti_pattern_note: A church gargoyle is NEVER aggressed in the churchyard without provoking it via desecration. Slayer tasks on them take place AWAY from the churchyard.

monsters.name: Orchard wight
monsters.examine: The spirit of a hanged orchard-thief.
bible: Heartlands law once hanged orchard-thieves from the tree they stole from. The practice stopped in the Great-Aunt Eastry reforms, but the last three hangings were never properly rested — no priest, no bell. Their spirits still climb the apple trees at dusk.

An orchard wight will accept an offering of a single, perfect apple left at the roots. Anything less is an insult; anything more is greed; both provoke it. The gift must be this year's fruit. Last year's apple is read as mockery.
Killing a wight restores the tree to ordinary fruiting but costs the player a month of bad luck at any Heartlands fair-day game. This is not superstition. The fair stall-holders remember faces.
monsters.habitat: old orchard trees at dusk, particularly the Greyling orchard north of town
monsters.reagent_callout: Drops orchard-wight rope (hemp noose fragment) which combines with a normal whip to forge the 'unburdened whip' (+1 defensive reach, slayer-niche only).

monsters.name: Marsh ratler
monsters.examine: Part rat, part snake — all mean.
bible: Marsh ratlers breed in the flooded corners of the Heartlands rice paddies, a crop the Sootworks recruiter tried to introduce in the drought year and nobody would plant again. The ratlers stayed.
They have the body of a rat and the neck of a grass snake. They hunt frogs and, when starved, children's fingers — not children; they are not ambitious.
A country-cure for the bite is wormwood poultice and a stern scolding. Most farm kids know the cure by age seven, and enforce the scolding part on each other.
monsters.habitat: drainage ditches, abandoned rice paddies, marshy field corners
monsters.anti_pattern_note: the ratler is a one-step-up from the corn rat slayer task. Keep difficulty shallow but the lore specific.

monsters.name: Bellman shade
monsters.examine: He still walks his round. The bell is missing.
bible: Heartlands night-bellmen used to walk the streets between midnight and four, ringing the quarter-hour and calling the weather. The last living bellman died thirty-one years ago. Some nights, a shade still walks the route.
He is not hostile unless you are out past curfew and cannot name a reason. He will demand the reason in a voice that was probably kind once. Lying to him does not work; he can tell. Silence works.

The militia considers him a colleague. They do not shoo him. A brave and stupid recruit once tried to; he was found the next morning three streets over, with no memory of how he got there and a great fear of church bells.
monsters.habitat: Heartlands town streets between midnight and four
monsters.anti_pattern_note: curfew check is real. Players out after hours draw his aggro automatically.

monsters.name: Thresher golem
monsters.examine: A threshing floor that learned to walk.
bible: Built by a Sootworks inventor the last bad harvest, the Thresher 'Three' was meant to do the work of ten men at half the cost. It did. Then it kept going. It threshed a barn, then a field, then, by most accounts, a dog.

The Heartlands Assembly voted it decommissioned. The decommission vote was lost by one (the inventor's). Three now wanders the north fields on a three-week loop, threshing anything the size of a sheaf.
Farmers leave it wheat piles on its known path as tribute. This works. It is a peaceful relationship, except for the dog.
monsters.habitat: north Heartlands fields, a predictable three-week loop
monsters.reagent_callout: Drops a thresher gear (reagent) that combines with the Sootworks 'sharp-iron strap' to produce the Thresher cleaver (slayer-niche vs plant-type monsters in Veilwood).

monsters.name: Brickyard hound
monsters.examine: A brickyard dog that never got fed.
bible: Heartlands brickworks keep hounds to discourage kiln-thieves. When a brickyard fails — and the town has two that did — the hounds remain on the lot, fed by whoever remembers, fed by nobody after a season or two. They turn feral fast.
A brickyard hound is almost always red-eyed from the kiln dust, and carries a distinctive cough. Farmers hearing the cough at night sleep with a poker by the door.
Unlike wolves, they do not pack. Each brickyard hound considers itself a solo animal with a specific grudge. The grudge is roughly: 'you humans'.
monsters.habitat: abandoned brickyards, kiln-warmed ruins, cold-ash lots
monsters.anti_pattern_note: pairs with the brickyard wight in the same abandoned-yard encounter — but both are solo; do not pack them.

region_flavor_drops: Hedgerow pelt (reagent: Ranger Cloak at Veilwood fletcher)
Militia insignia (reagent: Heartlands watch-shield at Smith Kael)
Hedgelord pin (1/512 from Rat king / Hedgerow stalker — crafts Hedgelord's belt)
